In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvmet: fix use-after-free of the old registrant in nvmet_pr_preempt()

nvmet_pr_preempt() handles a preempt sent by the reservation holder by
changing the reservation type with nvmet_pr_update_reg_attr(), unless
the reservation is of an All Registrants type.  For the holder that
helper does not modify the registrant in place: it puts a copy on the
registrant list, points pr->holder to the copy and passes the old
registrant to kfree_rcu().

If the reservation type changed, nvmet_pr_preempt() then hands
&reg->hostid of that old registrant to nvmet_pr_resv_released().  Unless
the reservation released notification is masked, that function takes
subsys->lock and compares the host id against every controller of the
subsystem.  The caller only holds pr->pr_sem and is not in an RCU
read-side critical section, so nothing keeps the old registrant alive
while it is read.

The result is a read of 16 freed bytes that decides which controllers
get the notification.  Found by code inspection.  kfree_rcu() defers
the free, so it usually happens after the read; when the pending free
is forced to run before the read, KASAN reports the host id as freed
memory.

Pass the host id of the controller that sent the command instead.  The
registrant was looked up by that host id, and the controller outlives
the request.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

platform/x86: asus-wmi: fix use-after-free unregistering kbd_led led

kbd_led_update_all() registers asus->kbd_led with
devm_led_classdev_register() on the platform device, but kbd_led is
embedded in struct asus_wmi, which asus_wmi_remove() frees at its end.
The driver core calls .remove() before devres_release_all(), so the
deferred devres release runs led_classdev_unregister() on memory that
has already been freed. Whether that faults depends on whether the
slab has been reused in between, which makes the crash on module
unload intermittent and silently corrupts the led classdev state in
the remaining runs.

Unregister the led classdev explicitly in asus_wmi_led_exit(), after
the led workqueue has been destroyed: kbd_led_work can then neither
run nor be queued anymore, since asus_ref.asus is NULL too, so
kbd_led_registered is stable and the classdev can be released while
the memory embedding it is still alive. devm_led_classdev_unregister()
also drops the devres entry, leaving nothing to run at unbind cleanup
time; it warns when no devres entry exists, hence the
kbd_led_registered check.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

PM: EM: Fix use-after-free of perf domain in netlink doit handlers

The doit handlers dropped em_pd_list_mutex before dereferencing the
perf domain, so a concurrent device unregister could free it while the
reply was being built.

Encode the reply from em_perf_domain_for_id() callbacks, which run
under the mutex, and allocate the skb outside of it, like the dumpit
path already does.

This issue was found by an in-house static analysis tool.

nothing ties the lifetime of that structure to the cdev: pps_gen is
freed by the release function of its device, and an open file holds a
device reference only until pps_gen_cdev_release() drops it.

When the generator is unregistered while /dev/pps-genN is open, that
put_device() drops the last reference and frees pps_gen, and __fput()
then calls cdev_put() on the freed cdev:

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

rapidio: mport_cdev: fix use-after-free in mport_mm_close()

A use-after-free vulnerability was identified in mport_mm_close() in
drivers/rapidio/devices/rio_mport_cdev.c, identical to the pattern
previously addressed in dma_req_free().

This is observable from userspace when an application creates an mmap
mapping via the RapidIO character device and subsequently unmaps it (or
terminates, triggering exit_mmap()).  During munmap, mport_mm_close() is
invoked and drops the mapping reference via kref_put().

If kref_put() drops the last reference, mport_release_mapping() is called,
which frees the underlying rio_mport_mapping structure.  The subsequent
mutex_unlock() then dereferences map->md to unlock buf_mutex, leading to a
use-after-free:

   mport_mm_close()
     -> mutex_lock(&map->md->buf_mutex);
     ...
     -> kref_put(&map->ref, mport_release_mapping); /* map is freed */
     -> mutex_unlock(&map->md->buf_mutex);          /* UAF: map used */

Fix this by caching map->md before kref_put() and using the cached pointer
for mutex unlocking, ensuring that freed memory is not accessed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

RDMA/irdma: avoid use-after-free in icrdma_remove

icrdma_remove() dereferences iwdev after calling
irdma_ib_unregister_device():

  irdma_ib_unregister_device(iwdev)
    -> ib_unregister_device(&iwdev->ibdev)
      -> __ib_unregister_device()
        -> ib_dealloc_device()

irdma registers irdma_ib_dealloc_device() as the dealloc_driver
callback in its ib_device_ops. The RDMA core explicitly documents
ib_unregister_device() that when ops.dealloc_driver is used, ib_dev
will be freed upon return from the function.

The ib_device is embedded in struct irdma_device and iwdev itself was
allocated by ib_alloc_device(irdma_device, ibdev). Consequently, once
irdma_ib_unregister_device() returns, iwdev must no longer be
dereferenced.

However, icrdma_remove() currently accesses iwdev->rf afterwards when
deinitializing interrupts, destroying ah_tbl_lock, and freeing rf.
Although the final ib_device storage is released with kfree_rcu(), the
object lifetime has already ended and callers must not rely on the RCU
grace period to continue dereferencing iwdev.

Save iwdev->rf before unregistering the RDMA device and use the saved
pointer for the remaining cleanup.

This issue was found by manual code inspection.

and leaves the uobject on the ufile list, but the dma_buf is freed as
soon as the release returns. The cleanup then destroys the uobject and
uses the freed dma_buf:

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sched_ext: Fix use-after-free of a local reenq node left on an inactive cpu

A local DSQ reenq is queued on the rq through a per-sched node and run from
deferred work. When the reenq is requested from dispatch, the work is a
balance callback queued once dispatch is done. A cpu going down installs
balance push early in its teardown, and queue_balance_callback() refuses new
callbacks from then on. ops.dispatch() keeps running on that cpu until the
rq goes offline after an RCU grace period, so a reenq it requests in that
window may never run. The IMMED handling in dispatch_one() requests one the
same way.

A reenq requested from elsewhere for a cpu that is already offline goes
through irq_work_queue_on(), which warns, and its work doesn't run until the
cpu comes back.

Either way the node stays on the rq's list. When the scheduler is freed,
scx_sched_free_rcu_work() warns and frees the pcpu with the node still
linked, and the list is walked again once the cpu comes back.

An inactive cpu's local DSQ holds only tasks that are bound to it or are
being moved off, so the reenq is pointless. Ignore reenqs of an inactive
cpu's local DSQ.

The test is lockless. The hotplug thread of a cpu going down runs on that
cpu, and it marks the cpu inactive before it installs balance push. A
dispatch on the cpu runs to completion before that thread can run there, so
a dispatch that saw the cpu active has queued its callback by then. Requests
from outside dispatch run from the wakeup path or through irq_work, which
balance push doesn't affect. The grace period after the cpu goes inactive
waits for any requester that saw it active, so that irq_work is queued while
the cpu is online.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix use-after-free in cifs_ses_add_channel()

The error path of cifs_ses_add_channel() calls cifs_put_tcp_session()
before cifs_chan_clear_need_reconnect().  The latter reaches
cifs_ses_get_chan_index(), which dereferences server->terminate; if
the put was the final reference, TCP_Server_Info is already freed and
this is a use-after-free.  Same put-then-use pattern as the recently
fixed sibling in commit 717e0a25036b ("cifs: Fix server use-after-free
in cifs_chan_skip_or_disable()").

Move the put last, but do not read chan->server after dropping
chan_lock: chan points into ses->chans[], and once chan_count is
decremented a concurrent add_channel can reuse the slot and overwrite
the pointer, so the put would act on the new channel's server.  Cache
the pointer under chan_lock, clear the reconnect bit and decrement
chan_count while still holding the reference, and release it after
the unlock.

This issue was discovered by Tencent CodeBuddy Security.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix use-after-free infoleak via the readdir resume name

CIFSFindNext() copies the resume name that cifs_save_resume_key()
recorded from the last entry of the previous response into its request;
psrch_inf->presume_name points into the response buffer that entry came
from, and nothing ever clears it. find_cifs_entry() records a new
name only from a response with a usable last entry, and cifs_readdir()
only from an entry it walks to, so a response that carries no entries
and leaves last_entry NULL, because CIFSFindFirst() or CIFSFindNext()
rejected LastNameOffset, refreshes neither and presume_name keeps
pointing into the previous response. That buffer has already been
released: by CIFSFindNext() before it installs the new response, or by

name either and can then fail in initiate_cifs_search() before a new

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

spmi: Fix potential use-after-free by grabbing of_node reference

As noticed by Sashiko during a review run of an unrelated patch,
in of_spmi_register_devices(), for_each_available_child_of_node()
is used to loop through children, and to also assign a node to a
newly created SPMI child device.

Problem is that the refcount is dropped at every iteration so, in

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

SUNRPC: fix netns use-after-free in write_gssp()

While fuzzing with a customized syzkaller, I hit a refcount warning in
xprt_alloc(), reached from a write to /proc/net/rpc/use-gss-proxy:

  refcount_t: addition on 0; use-after-free.
  WARNING: lib/refcount.c:25 at refcount_warn_saturate+0xf8/0x120
  CPU: 0 PID: 10404 Comm: syz.0.17 Not tainted 7.3.0-rc1-00096-gcfebfd3db73d
  Call Trace:
   <TASK>
   xprt_alloc+0x83f/0x9d0
   xs_setup_xprt+0xaf/0x3c0
   xs_setup_local+0x47/0x7f0
   xprt_create_transport+0x16c/0x730
   rpc_create+0x38e/0x7f0
   gssp_rpc_create+0xe2/0x180
   set_gssp_clnt+0xba/0x1b0
   write_gssp+0x200/0x310
   proc_reg_write+0x240/0x330
   vfs_write+0x2aa/0x1050
   ksys_write+0x12a/0x250
   do_syscall_64+0x117/0x750
   entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f
   </TASK>

create_use_gss_proxy_proc_entry() stores the struct net pointer as the
proc entry's private data without taking a reference on it, and an open
file descriptor does not pin the namespace either, as procfs only pins
the proc_dir_entry. write_gssp() reads that pointer back with
pde_data() and hands it to set_gssp_clnt(), which reaches xprt_init():

	xprt->xprt_net = get_net_track(net, &xprt->ns_tracker, GFP_KERNEL);

get_net_track() -> get_net() -> refcount_inc() is unconditional, so
rpc_create() assumes its caller holds a reference on args.net.
write_gssp() does not.

Dropping the last ns.count reference does not make the file go away.
__put_net() only queues cleanup_net() on a workqueue, and the
remove_proc_entry() that fences off further writes runs from the
rpcsec_gss pernet .exit method, that is, from inside cleanup_net(). A
write landing between those two points increments a refcount that is
already zero. cleanup_net() does not re-read ns.count, so the namespace
is freed anyway and the rpc_xprt -- along with the AF_LOCAL socket
opened for it -- is left pointing at freed memory. The resurrected
count is visible to the rest of that teardown too: with
CONFIG_IPV6_MROUTE the same cleanup_net() worker then trips
!mr_can_free_table() in ip6mr_free_table(), which tests check_net() on
the namespace it is freeing.

It reduces to opening /proc/net/rpc/use-gss-proxy inside a new network
namespace, calling setns() back to the original one to drop the last
reference, and then writing "1" to the still-open descriptor.

Take the reference in write_gssp() itself and refuse the write when the
namespace is already gone. This is what procfs does for every other
/proc/net file: get_proc_net() is maybe_get_net(PDE_NET(PDE(inode)))
and seq_open_net() returns -ENXIO when it fails. PDE_NET() cannot be
reused here because the parent directory /proc/net/rpc carries no
namespace pointer. Adding a .pre_exit to rpcsec_gss_net_ops so the
entry is removed earlier would only narrow the window, since pre_exit
also runs from cleanup_net().

Live namespaces are unaffected: a write still returns the error from
set_gssp_clnt(), a write of "2" still returns -EINVAL, and reads are
untouched.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: b43: fix use-after-free in b43_bcma_remove()

device of. b43_bcma_remove() then reads wldev->dev again to free the bus

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

cgroup: serialize migrations of newly forked processes

With favordynmods enabled, a cgroup.procs migration takes the target
threadgroup's cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem for writing. A process fork holds
the forking threadgroup's semaphore for reading. These are different
semaphores when fork creates a new process.

copy_process() publishes the child's PID before cgroup_post_fork() links
the child to its css_set. A writer can find the child in that interval,
take its uncontended semaphore, and migrate it while child->cgroups still
points to init_css_set and child->cg_list is empty. Migration links the
node into init_css_set.mg_tasks. cgroup_post_fork() then adds the same
node to the intended css_set as though it were unlinked, corrupting both
task lists and their css_set ownership.

This regresses the fork/migration race fixed by commit b12b533fa523
("cgroups: add lock for child->cgroups in cgroup_post_fork()") and
restored again in 2012 after the lock had been removed. The old task_lock
protection was later superseded by global css_set and cgroup threadgroup
locking. The change identified by the Fixes tag narrowed only the migration
side back to a per-threadgroup lock, recreating the different-process
exclusion failure.

Take the new threadgroup's semaphore for reading before the child becomes
visible and hold it through cgroup_post_fork(). Use a nested lock subclass
because fork already holds the parent's semaphore. CLONE_THREAD children
share the parent's signal_struct and remain covered by the existing lock.
Migrations of unrelated, fully initialized threadgroups remain concurrent.

An AI coding assistant was used to identify and reproduce the regression
and to develop and test this fix.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: verify transform SessionId matches the decrypted header

When an encrypted request comes in, the decryption key is picked by
the SessionId in the transform header, but the request is then
authorized under whatever session the decrypted inner header names.
Nothing ever compares the two, so on a connection with more than
one session a client can get a request decrypted with one session's
key and run it as another session. Encrypted requests are exempt
from signing too, so a valid AEAD tag is the only proof of session
identity, and it is checked against the wrong session.

MS-SMB2 says the server must check that the transform SessionId
matches the one in the decrypted SMB2 header and treat a mismatch
as a protocol error. Add that check in __handle_ksmbd_work() after
decryption, before dispatching: the message has to be at least one
fixed SMB2 header, the first operation must not set
SMB2_FLAGS_RELATED_OPERATIONS and its SessionId must match the
transform SessionId, and every following non-related operation in
a compound chain must carry the same SessionId. NextCommand
offsets must be 8-byte aligned and stay inside the message; the
bounds check is done by subtraction so it cannot wrap.

When the decrypted payload is a compression transform, the
existing decompression step runs first and the decompressed SMB2
message is checked instead, since a compression transform header
carries no SessionId.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: validate security descriptor offsets before pointer arithmetic

parse_sec_desc() constructs SID and DACL pointers by adding untrusted
32-bit offsets to the security descriptor before checking their bounds.
The existing checks reject offsets into the descriptor header, but do
not reject offsets beyond the descriptor's length.

On a 32-bit kernel, a large offset can wrap the pointer before the
descriptor. The end-only checks in parse_sid() and parse_dacl() can then
accept it, allowing an authenticated SMB2 SET_INFO request to access
memory outside the security descriptor and fault the kernel.

Check each nonzero offset against acl_len before constructing its
pointer. Initialize the optional owner and group SID pointers to NULL
so an omitted SID remains absent when parsing the DACL.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: validate AppInstanceId takeover target

AppInstanceId lookup currently selects the first open with the matching
identifier. CREATE for an unrelated share or path can therefore
force-close another session's open before authorization of the new
target. Matching only the base path also conflates alternate data streams
with the unnamed stream.

MS-SMB2 requires the old open to match the share and path, belong to a
different ClientGuid, and be closed only when the requester has
GENERIC_READ access. Search all opens with the ID and match share,
resolved path, stream, and the current connection's client GUID. Retain a
share configuration reference in ksmbd_file and reuse its name instead of
allocating a name for every open. This keeps matching safe during tree
connection teardown and preserves name-based matching across configuration
updates.

Refresh the share reference on durable reconnect and restore the old
reference if reopening fails. Serialize connection and share comparisons
with durable disconnect/reconnect, and recheck the target before closing
it. Keep the original ClientGuid for durable replay and lease checks.

Check AppInstanceVersion before querying access, even when GENERIC_READ
is absent, and before disconnected delete-on-close cleanup. Rejected
CREATE must leave other durable opens untouched. Calculate maximal access
on the matched open's referenced path so a rename cannot substitute another
file's authorization. Require read access with the effective VFS
credentials as well as the NT DACL before takeover. Access denial only
skips takeover and leaves CREATE to its normal access checks. Restore
filesystem credentials before returning a takeover error.

Handle takeover before checking FILE_CREATE collisions, and re-resolve
the path after closing the old open. This lets delete-on-close remove the
old file before a new one is created. Include SYNCHRONIZE in the baseline
maximal-access mask so read-only files report GENERIC_READ correctly.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: prevent stale data from being written by SMB2 WRITE requests

Initialize the compatibility byte in request buffers without zeroing
the entire allocation. Keep the one-byte compatibility exception for
SMB2 messages so valid zero-length WRITE requests remain compatible,
and validate the data range in the WRITE handlers against the current
compound request before accessing it.

This prevents stale request-buffer data from being written to files or
sent to IPC pipes.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: prevent share root removal through empty paths

A FileLinkInformation request can supply "/" as the new link name.
smb2_get_name() strips the trailing slash and passes an empty string to
ksmbd_vfs_kern_path_start_removing().

ksmbd_vfs_path_lookup() resolves an empty pathname as the configured share
path, without LOOKUP_BENEATH. With ReplaceIfExists set, smb2_create_link()
can therefore remove the share root from its parent before link creation
fails. An authenticated client with a writable share and DELETE access to
a file can trigger this if the share root is empty and the mapped user
has write and search permission on its parent directory.

Return -EINVAL for empty pathnames when for_remove is set, before
resolving the share path or acquiring removal resources. Ordinary lookups
continue to accept empty pathnames for opening the share root.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: prevent session binding in compound requests

A failed multichannel binding can retain its target session on the work
item so that the error response can be signed. Subsequent compound
commands can then use that session together with a tree connection left
over from an earlier command.

Limit binding SESSION_SETUP requests to standalone messages during
message validation, before smb2_sess_setup() can replace work->sess.
Check both NextCommand and the current request offset to cover binding
in the first, middle and last positions of a compound. The existing
validation error path returns STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER and stops
processing the remaining commands.

This intentionally limits support for compounded binding. It is not a
protocol requirement that binding be standalone. Standalone binding and
non-binding compounds retain their existing behavior, without changing
session, tree or response encryption handling.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: preserve unreadable named streams on open

A write-only client can open an existing named stream with FILE_OPEN_IF
without permission to read the underlying file. The case-insensitive
lookup finds the xattr name, but querying its value length then fails
with -EACCES. smb2_set_stream_name_xattr() treats every negative result
as a missing stream and replaces the existing xattr with an empty value.

A failed xattr list is not proof that the stream is absent either:
for example, -ENOMEM can lead to the same empty replacement. Preserve
listing errors and create a stream only for -ENOENT or -ENODATA. The
latter can occur if the xattr is removed between listing its name and
querying its value. Return other lookup errors without changing the
stream.

A write-only FILE_OPEN now reports access denied instead of name not
found. FILE_OVERWRITE_IF and FILE_SUPERSEDE on an unreadable stream
also fail instead of appearing to replace it. Stream writes and EOF
changes already need to read the old value, so such handles cannot
update the stream after opening either.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: ignore network devices of other namespaces

With no interface list configured, ksmbd binds every interface that
comes up. ksmbd_netdev_event() does not look at the device's namespace,
and create_socket() opens the listener in the namespace of the task
raising NETDEV_UP. A container with its own address on a bridge brings
up its interface and finds port 445 in its namespace already taken by
ksmbd, so an SMB server running inside the container fails with
"Address already in use".

Interfaces are also matched by name only, so a container's eth0 going
down would stop the listener on the host's eth0.

Only handle netdev events for devices in init_net.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix session reference leak on compounded SESSION_SETUP

A compound request can place SESSION_SETUP after another command. That
earlier command leaves a reference to its session in work->sess.
smb2_sess_setup() then overwrites work->sess with the session it looks up
or creates, and the dispatcher later puts work->sess only once. The
inherited reference is never dropped. That leaks the session, together
with its setup connection and socket, and every repeat of the compound
leaks another.

  unreferenced object (size 512):
    __kmalloc_cache_noprof+0x32c/0x3a0
    ksmbd_smb2_session_create+0xf6/0x9c0 [ksmbd]
    smb2_sess_setup+0xda4/0x6280 [ksmbd]
    handle_ksmbd_work+0x88c/0x1cb0 [ksmbd]

Save the inherited session on entry. After the request has been
processed, release it once, but only when smb2_sess_setup() has replaced
work->sess with its own session or cleared it. Do this after
ksmbd_conn_unlock() so the put does not run under srv_mutex. An error path
may instead leave the inherited session in work->sess. Keep it there, so
the dispatcher still puts it and the error response is still signed or
encrypted with it as before.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix parent dentry lifetime in directory enumeration

ksmbd_populate_dot_dotdot_entries() builds the ".." entry from
the open directory's d_parent and passes that pointer to
ksmbd_vfs_fill_dentry_attrs() without taking a reference. That pointer
is only valid while the directory stays under this parent. If a
concurrent rename moves the directory elsewhere, the old parent loses
its last reference; a following rmdir then turns it into a negative
dentry with d_inode cleared, and after the RCU grace period the dentry
itself is freed. The worker still holds the raw pointer and
dereferences d_inode through vfs_getattr() and vfs_getxattr().

A remote SMB client, authenticated or guest, triggers this by listing
a directory while that directory is moved under a new parent and the
old parent is deleted. It can be done by the client itself with write
access or by other concurrent writers, triggering null-ptr-deref and
slab-use-after-free on a KASAN build.

  KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range
      [0x0000000000000000-0x0000000000000007]
  Workqueue: ksmbd-io handle_ksmbd_work
  RIP: 0010:xattr_permission+0x9d/0x160
  Call Trace:
   vfs_getxattr+0x9c/0x1b0
   ksmbd_vfs_getxattr+0x82/0x100
   ksmbd_vfs_get_dos_attrib_xattr+0x7f/0x130
   ksmbd_vfs_fill_dentry_attrs+0x435/0x650
   ksmbd_populate_dot_dotdot_entries+0x25e/0x630
   smb2_query_dir+0xcf9/0x1a20
   handle_ksmbd_work+0x5f1/0x1c80
   process_one_work+0x90b/0x19d0

Fix by using the dentry reference counting APIs: take the parent with
dget_parent(), take a matching dget() on ".", and dput() the dentry
once ksmbd_vfs_fill_dentry_attrs() has returned or the pattern does
not match.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix OOB read and cross-share confusion in ksmbd_validate_name_reconnect()

ksmbd_validate_name_reconnect() indexes
ab_pathname[share->path_sz + 1] without checking that the path is
longer than share->path_sz + 1 (d_path() fills the buffer from the
end). A durable fp is not bound to its original share, so a client
can preserve a file from a short-path share and reconnect it on a
long-path share, making strcmp() read past the PATH_MAX buffer -
with a long enough share path this oopses the kernel, and on a
mapped page it also gives a byte-equality oracle on adjacent heap
(the reconnect succeeds exactly when the out-of-bounds string
equals the requested name). A same-share variant with the durable
fp at the share root reads 1 byte past the buffer
(strlen(ab_pathname) == share->path_sz).

Check before comparing: the path must be longer than share->path_sz,
it must start with share->path, and the next character must be '/'.
The share root itself is accepted only for an empty name.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: deny access for an empty DACL instead of granting the request

smb_check_perm_dacl() returns the access mask it computes to the SMB2
CREATE handler, which uses it as the granted access for the open. For a
security descriptor whose DACL is present but contains no ACEs, the
function is supposed to deny access: an empty (non-NULL) DACL grants no
access to anyone except the object owner's implicit READ_CONTROL and
WRITE_DAC (MS-DTYP 2.4.5).

The empty-DACL branch only denies when both

  - the DACL has no trailing bytes (pdacl_size == sizeof(struct smb_acl)),
    and
  - the request contains bits beyond READ_CONTROL / WRITE_DAC.

In every other case it takes the shared "goto err_out" with rc still 0,
which returns success without modifying *pdaccess, so the caller grants
the full requested access. Three problems follow:

  - The READ_CONTROL / WRITE_DAC carve-out models the owner's implicit
    rights, but the check runs before is_owner is computed, so those
    rights are handed to *every* caller, not just the owner. For
    READ_CONTROL the SMB2 CREATE path does not fall back to
    inode_permission(), so any user can read the security descriptor of
    an object whose empty DACL is meant to deny them.

  - A request of exactly READ_CONTROL and/or WRITE_DAC is granted to any
    caller. WRITE_DAC lets the handle rewrite the DACL.

  - A DACL that declares zero ACEs but carries trailing bytes
    (pdacl_size > sizeof(struct smb_acl)) skips the deny entirely and is
    granted whatever was requested.

On shares where the NT ACL is the authoritative access control -- e.g.
"force user" shares, where every client maps to one POSIX identity so
POSIX cannot distinguish users -- this is an access-control bypass.

Compute is_owner before the empty-DACL branch and deny access from an
empty DACL unless the caller is the owner requesting no more than
READ_CONTROL / WRITE_DAC.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

backlight: qcom-wled: Fix NULL pointer dereference in wled_remove()

wled_probe() doesn't set the driver data for the platform device.
As a result, platform_get_drvdata() in wled_remove() will return NULL,
and the first dereference of it crashes on unbind.

Set the platform device driver data in wled_probe().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Drivers: hv: vmbus: Bounds check the shared ring buffer indices

In a CoCo VM the host is untrusted. Since the VMBus ring buffer read and
write indices live in shared memory, the guest has to treat both as
potentially malicious.

hv_ringbuffer_write() copies into the ring at write_index with no bounds
checking, so the host can make the guest write packet data at any offset
up to 4 GiB past the start of the ring buffer. read_index matters too:
the available space derived from both indices is the only bound on how
much is copied, and an out-of-range index can make it far larger than
the ring.

The fix is to validate both indices before use and to use the validated
snapshot instead of re-accessing. For invalid indices,
hv_ringbuffer_write() logs and returns -EIO.

One re-read of write_index is left unchecked in this patch:
hv_get_ring_bufferindices() fetches it again for the prev_indices
trailer. The value is only returned to the host and is not used as an
offset or length for indexing. Since this is not a security issue, it is
addressed later in the series.

Open-coding the bytes available arithmetic keeps the fix free of
prerequisites; a later patch refactors it into a helper function.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

driver core: take parent lock on deferred probe

USB interfaces should be probed with the parent USB device lock held,
but this is not honoured when probe is deferred.

Add a new bus_probe_device_deferred() helper to handle deferred probe
where the parent device lock is not held.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/sched: cls_flower: avoid stale mask references after delete

Flower releases a mask reference when a filter is removed from the
classifier. The filter object can remain alive while dump, walk, or
hardware reoffload paths hold a reference to it. Those paths can then
dereference f->mask after the mask has already been released.

Keep the mask reference until the filter reference count reaches zero.
Release the mask synchronously from the final __fl_put() while the caller
still holds the tcf_proto reference, and leave the existing RCU work to
free the mask. This keeps the mask available to every reader that still
holds the filter.

The filter is still removed from the classifier indexes immediately.
Therefore, a deleted filter can temporarily retain an otherwise empty
mask; fl_delete() uses the handle IDR, rather than the mask list, to
determine whether the classifier has become empty.

Failed mask assignment can leave fnew->mask as an error or borrowed
pointer without an owned mask reference. Clear it before the common
failure path so the final put cannot release an unowned reference.

This fix does not add fields, snapshots, or per-filter memory.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

thunderbolt: Do not RPM complete unrelated subtrees on unplug

When a Thunderbolt device is unplugged, that switch and every switch
subsequent to it on the bus device list is `complete()`d, not just its
child devices. In the case of multiple domains, it may cause, eg, an
attempt to `complete()` the uninitialized domain 1 root switch RPM
completion on unplug of a switch from domain 0 (though ordering is not
guaranteed numerically sorted).

I initially noticed this issue on a Dell XPS9720 when the system would
seem to sporadically not wake after unplugging a Thunderbolt dock. I
tried multiple kernel versions including v7.2.7 and v7.3-rc4 to see if
that resolved the issue, but the issue persisted. Eventually I found
that I could consistently generate a kernel Oops reporting a page fault
at 0xffff_ffff_ffff_fff8 on unplug from one side of the laptop and went
bug hunting. I became suspicious of the `bus_for_each_dev()` walk that I
ultimately ended up changing. To confirm this issue, I did an eBPF trace
of `bus_for_each_dev()`, `complete_rpm()`, and `complete()` while
unplugging in a variety of situations and found that an unplug from
domain 0 tries to `complete_rpm()` domain 1's switch, whose RPM
completion is not initialized and thus is holding a null wait-list
pointer, triggering the page fault.

Here are the key sections of that eBPF trace. Note that HEAD denotes the
completion's own wait-list HEAD:

```
RESCAN_ENTER domain=0

COMPLETE rescan_domain=0 target=0-1 target_domain=0
         route=0x1 parent=0-0 unplugged=1
COMPLETION done=0 head=HEAD next=HEAD prev=HEAD

BUS_WALK domain=0 start=0-1 callback=complete_rpm
CALLBACK_ENTER rescan_domain=0 dev=1-0 parent=domain1 is_switch=1

COMPLETE rescan_domain=0 target=1-0 target_domain=1
         route=0x0 parent=domain1 unplugged=0
COMPLETION done=0 head=HEAD next=0 prev=0

        complete+5
        complete_rpm+43
        bus_for_each_dev+133
        icm_free_unplugged_children+250
        icm_rescan_work+42
```

This patch gates the `complete()` on an additional condition - that the
Thunderbolt domain matches the domain of the device that was unplugged.

I only have a single system with multiple Thunderbolt domains - the Dell
XPS9720. I am consistently able to reproduce the Oops on that system.
Since running with this patch, I have not seen the Oops reoccur. I have
also tested it on a Thinkpad X1-Gen12, and that system boots and runs
well with it, but it only has a single Thunderbolt domain, so it does
not exercise the multi-domain failure case.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix early procfs exposure race

Currently, init_cifs() calls cifs_proc_init() near the beginning of
the function, before INIT_LIST_HEAD, leading to a momentarily
uninitialized, but exposed, procfs. If a userspace process reads this
empty procfs, iterating over a zeroed list_head leads to a NULL
pointer dereference and a kernel oops/panic.

For example, if a delay is added between cifs_proc_init() and
INIT_LIST_HEAD, and a userspace process is polling
/proc/fs/cifs/DebugData, the following oops occurs:

BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000608
Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP PTI
CPU: 0 UID: 0 PID: 3477 Comm: cat Not tainted
7.3.0-02212-g4df4d2a577db-dirty #6 PREEMPT(lazy)
RIP: 0010:cifs_debug_data_proc_show+0x103/0xd80 [cifs]
Call Trace:
<TASK>
 ? seq_read_iter+0x86/0x400
 ? seq_read_iter+0x86/0x400
 seq_read_iter+0x183/0x400
 proc_reg_read_iter+0x62/0x90
 copy_splice_read+0x215/0x310
 splice_file_to_pipe+0xec/0x1c0
 do_splice+0x4b8/0x780
 __se_sys_splice+0x18f/0x250
 do_syscall_64+0x109/0x330
 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f
</TASK>

Fix this by moving cifs_proc_init() down in init_cifs(), ensuring it runs
only after all internal lists, locks, counters, and workqueues are fully
ready, but before registering the filesystem. Update the error cleanup
ladder and exit_cifs() to maintain proper LIFO order.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: do not pass a NULL buf to is_oplock_break()

receive_encrypted_read() sets *num_mids = 1 and never writes the
caller's bufs[]. Offload returns -1 with *num_mids = 0, so the
demultiplex thread skips the frame. The inline decrypt path
returns 0 even when smb2_find_mid() fails.

cifs_demultiplex_thread() then treats mids[i] == NULL as an
oplock break and calls is_oplock_break(bufs[i], server) with
bufs[i] still NULL. smb2_is_valid_oplock_break() reads
hdr.Command at offset 12 and oopses.

A large encrypted READ whose MessageId does not match is enough
to panic cifsd.

    Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address
    0xdffffc0000000001: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI
    KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range
    [0x0000000000000008-0x000000000000000f]
    CPU: 0 PID: 100 Comm: cifsd
    RIP: smb2_is_valid_oplock_break+0xc8/0x2270 [cifs]
    cifs_demultiplex_thread
    Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception

Return -1 when inline decrypt finds no mid, and skip
is_oplock_break() plus the unknown-frame dump when bufs[i]
is NULL. receive_encrypted_standard() already assigns
bufs[*num_mids].

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: pin owning modules for open debugfs files

The OCFS2 debugfs file operation tables do not set owner. The
full debugfs proxy obtains real_fops with fops_get() at open and
keeps it until final release. Without an owner, this does not acquire
a reference to the module containing the table and its callbacks.
Removing the debugfs entries does not drain retained open files.

An open connected_nodes file can therefore outlive ocfs2_nodemanager
and make full_proxy_release() read real_fops->release from freed
module memory. Heming also reproduced the issue with fs_state and
asked for the other OCFS2 debugfs operation tables to be checked.

Set owner to THIS_MODULE in all eleven explicit debugfs operation
tables: five in ocfs2_nodemanager, four in ocfs2_dlm, and two in
ocfs2. The existing debugfs get/put pair then holds the appropriate
module until final release. Leave the open, read and release callbacks
unchanged. The blockcheck table already sets owner through
DEFINE_DEBUGFS_ATTRIBUTE(), so it needs no change.

The original controlled test used an unloadable OCFS2 module and
case-local probe filters without changing the candidate open, unload
or release logic. Closing a retained connected_nodes file after
normal unload produced:

  BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: fffffbfff804cfef
  Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI
  RIP: 0010:full_proxy_release+0xbf/0x190
  Call Trace:
   <TASK>
   __fput+0x39a/0xa60
   fput_close_sync+0xff/0x200
   __x64_sys_close+0x8c/0xf0
   do_syscall_64+0x114/0x620
   entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f
   </TASK>

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: drain quorum work before removing the cluster

The configured cluster must remain available until an in-flight quorum
decision has finished using its fencing method.  o2quo_make_decision()
drops qs_lock before calling o2quo_fence_self(), which marks heartbeat
regions for unclean stop and then reads
o2nm_single_cluster->cl_fence_method.  Cluster removal clears the
singleton without waiting for this independent system-workqueue item.

When a failed-quorum decision overlaps removal of the heartbeat regions,
nodes and cluster through configfs, the worker can be preempted after
marking the regions and resume after the singleton has been cleared:

  Quorum worker                     Configfs removal
  select fence; drop qs_lock
  o2hb_stop_all_regions()
                                    remove regions; join heartbeat threads
                                    remove nodes; stop o2net
                                    clear singleton; release cluster
  read cl_fence_method

The resumed read dereferences NULL instead of applying the configured
fencing method. The heartbeat thread's dependency protects the local
node only until the thread exits, and draining o2net does not wait for
qs_work.

Add o2quo_flush_work() to drain pending or running quorum decisions
before clearing the singleton in o2nm_cluster_group_drop_item(). By
this point the heartbeat regions and nodes have been removed, so their
work publishers are stopped. The worker can finish while the cluster
and its configured fencing method remain available. It does not acquire
the configfs mutex held by the removal path.

Keep o2quo_exit() as the counterpart of o2quo_init() for module teardown
and initialization failure, and have it call the same drain helper.
Cluster removal uses only the explicitly named drain operation.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/dlm: drain join handlers before releasing module text

The code for a registered DLM handler must remain resident until its
last invocation finishes. dlm_unregister_net_handlers() only removes
dlm_join_handlers from the o2net registry. o2net_handler_get() takes a
kref on the wrapper, but that reference does not pin ocfs2_dlm text.
o2net_process_message() calls nh_func after dropping o2net_handler_lock.

With CONFIG_OCFS2_FS_O2CB=m, ocfs2_dlm can be loaded independently of
ocfs2_stack_o2cb while nodemanager continues handling messages from a
configured, heartbeating peer. If no dependent module or module reference
prevents normal unload, the following ordering is possible:

  Receive worker                       Module unload
  --------------                       -------------
  o2net_handler_get()
    take wrapper kref
    drop handler lock
  <preempted>
                                       dlm_exit()
                                         unregister handlers
                                       release DLM module text
  call saved nh_func
    in released module text

Use o2net_unregister_and_flush_handler_list() in the shared DLM
unregister helper. It first prevents new lookups, then waits for the
ordered o2net workqueue to drain, including a concurrent destruction of
that queue. The acquired invocation therefore finishes before dlm_exit()
returns and the loader releases the callback code. The same helper
covers partial registration and dlm_init() error unwind before module
memory is released.

Skip the drain when the private join-handler list is empty. Early
dlm_init() failures can reach this helper before any handler has been
published. Partial-registration failure also reaches it a second time
after the first call has already unregistered and drained the list.
Neither case needs to take o2net_wq_mutex or drain unrelated work.
The list is changed only by serialized module init/exit paths; a
nonempty list still uses the full unregister-and-flush helper.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nfsd: fix race between client_info_show() and free_client()

client_info_show() renders /proc/fs/nfsd/clients/<id>/info and walks
clp->cl_sessions under clp->cl_lock to print each session's slot
counts.  free_client() tears down the same list without taking
cl_lock, and is the only unlocked mutator of cl_sessions.  A reader
can observe a client mid-teardown because get_nfsdfs_clp() pins the
nfs4_client but not its sessions: free_client() frees every session
before calling nfsd_client_rmdir(), so an in-flight seq_file reader
can follow a list_del()'d node whose ->next now holds LIST_POISON1
and take a general protection fault:

  Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address
        0xdead00000000014c
  CPU: 1 UID: 0 PID: 132488 Comm: cat
  RIP: 0010:client_info_show+0x2bf/0x3d0
  RAX: dead000000000100
  Call Trace:
   seq_read_iter+0x12a/0x4b0
   seq_read+0xf1/0x130
   vfs_read+0xbf/0x350
   ksys_read+0x6f/0xf0
   do_syscall_64+0x8b/0xcb0
   entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x76/0x7e
  Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception

Detach cl_sessions onto a local reaplist under cl_lock, then free the
sessions after dropping the lock.  Removing entries from cl_sessions
under cl_lock matches unhash_session(), and the detach-then-reap shape
matches how __destroy_client() reaps cl_delegations.  The sessions
cannot be freed while cl_lock is held, since free_session() calls
nfsd4_del_conns(), which re-acquires it.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: usb: pegasus: do not advance rx_skb->data on dropped frames

For the 0x8513 chip, read_bulk_callback() skips the 2-byte receive
header by advancing pegasus->rx_skb->data in place. This is done before
the pkt_len > PEGASUS_MTU check, and when that check drops the frame
the good path resubmits the same skb with the advanced rx_skb->data as
the transfer buffer, still PEGASUS_MTU bytes long.

Every frame with an oversized length field therefore moves the receive
buffer two more bytes towards the end of the skb data area. A device
that keeps sending such frames makes the host controller write received
data over skb_shared_info and past the end of the allocation, and the
corrupted skb_shared_info is used when the skb is eventually freed.
With an emulated device sending frames filled with 0x5a on a KASAN
kernel:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in dummy_timer+0xade/0x3f00 [dummy_hcd]
  Write of size 1536 at addr ffff888105821202 by task swapper/1/0
  ...
  Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xeb4b474b4b4b4b4c: 0000 [#1] PREEMPT SMP KASAN NOPTI
  KASAN: maybe wild-memory-access in range [0x5a5a5a5a5a5a5a60-0x5a5a5a5a5a5a5a67]
  RIP: 0010:skb_release_data+0x36f/0x800

Only skip the header with skb_reserve() once the frame is going to be
passed up, so the receive buffer always starts at the beginning of the
skb data area. Unlike the old pointer adjustment, skb_reserve() also
moves skb->tail, so the two header bytes now count against the buffer
size: lower the length limit for the 0x8513 accordingly, otherwise a
pkt_len of PEGASUS_MTU - 1 or PEGASUS_MTU would trip skb_over_panic().

Found by code review with LLM assistance and reproduced with an
emulated USB device (raw-gadget + dummy_hcd).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

media: usbtv: fix null-pointer dereference on disconnect

A null-pointer dereference can occur in usb_make_path() when called from
usbtv_querycap() (and other ioctl handlers) during device disconnection.

Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address
0xdffffc000000000a: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI
KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000050-0x0000000000000057]
RIP: 0010:usb_make_path include/linux/usb.h:985 [inline]
RIP: 0010:usbtv_querycap+0x9c/0x100
drivers/media/usb/usbtv/usbtv-video.c:612
...
Call Trace:
 <TASK>
 v4l_querycap+0x236/0x470 drivers/media/v4l2-core/v4l2-ioctl.c:1106
 __video_do_ioctl+0x8af/0xc70 drivers/media/v4l2-core/v4l2-ioctl.c:3133
 video_usercopy+0x860/0x1430 drivers/media/v4l2-core/v4l2-ioctl.c:3475
 v4l2_ioctl+0x18d/0x1e0 drivers/media/v4l2-core/v4l2-dev.c:366
 vfs_ioctl fs/ioctl.c:51 [inline]
 __do_sys_ioctl fs/ioctl.c:597 [inline]
 __se_sys_ioctl+0xfc/0x170 fs/ioctl.c:583
 do_syscall_x64 arch/x86/entry/syscall_64.c:63 [inline]
 do_syscall_64+0x174/0x580 arch/x86/entry/syscall_64.c:94

This happens due to a race condition between the USB device disconnect
routine (usbtv_disconnect()) and V4L2 ioctls. When the device is
disconnected, usbtv_disconnect() sets usbtv->udev = NULL without holding
the usbtv->v4l2_lock mutex. Concurrently, an ioctl handler like
usbtv_querycap() can be executing under the v4l2_lock and attempt to use
usbtv->udev, leading to a crash.

To fix this, move the usbtv->udev = NULL assignment into usbtv_video_free()
and protect it with mutex_lock(&usbtv->v4l2_lock). This ensures that no
non-queue ioctl handler can run concurrently with the pointer being
nullified. If an ioctl is already running, the mutex will block the
disconnect path until the ioctl finishes. If an ioctl is blocked waiting
for the lock, it will acquire it after the disconnect routine releases it,
but will then check video_is_registered() (which was cleared by
vb2_video_unregister_device()) and safely return -ENODEV.

Acquiring v4l2_lock after vb2_video_unregister_device() avoids
reintroducing a historical deadlock issue, and usbtv_audio_free() remains
safe as it is called before usbtv_video_free().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: serialize directory emptiness checks with readdir

SMB2 QUERY_DIRECTORY holds fp->readdir_lock while it calls iterate_dir()
on fp->filp. An SMB2 SET_INFO request with FILE_DISPOSITION_INFORMATION
can resolve the same FileId and call ksmbd_vfs_empty_dir() on the same
filp without that lock.

iterate_dir()'s inode read lock permits concurrent readers and does not
serialize per-file iterator state. ext4 stores its dx readdir cursor and
fname RB tree in file->private_data. Concurrent reset or refill can
therefore free a fname node while the other worker still traverses it or
retains its RB-tree link, resulting in use-after-free accesses.

An authenticated SMB client with list and delete rights on a directory in
a writable KSMBD share backed by ext4 can trigger this when the directory
takes the dx readdir path. The client overlaps an SMB2 QUERY_DIRECTORY
request with an SMB2 SET_INFO request carrying FILE_DISPOSITION_INFORMATION
on one live FileId.

In one x86_64 SMP KASAN multi-shot guest using ksmbd-for-next at
171df27077fb, the unmodified kernel reported a cross-worker use-after-free
before a panic. The first report's access and free stacks show the two
request paths directly (trimmed):

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in ext4_htree_store_dirent+0x488/0x550
  Read of size 8 by task kworker/2:0/29
  Workqueue: ksmbd-io handle_ksmbd_work
  Call Trace:
   ext4_htree_store_dirent+0x488/0x550
   htree_dirblock_to_tree+0x535/0x990
   ext4_htree_fill_tree+0x319/0xba0
   ext4_readdir+0x175a/0x2f40
   iterate_dir+0x1b6/0x630
   smb2_query_dir+0x1003/0x1cc0

  Freed by task 279:
   free_rb_tree_fname+0x67/0xc0
   ext4_readdir+0x13a9/0x2f40
   iterate_dir+0x1b6/0x630
   ksmbd_vfs_empty_dir+0xa2/0x100
   smb2_set_info+0x2ffa/0x45d0

Take fp->readdir_lock across the entire emptiness check. This places both
iterators over that handle's filp in the same lock domain while
preserving the disposition status handling. The exact code change
completed a warning-free x86_64 KASAN bzImage build. Tracing three request
pairs showed that the two iterate_dir() calls no longer overlapped and the
expected statuses were preserved. A further 1,600 reproducer iterations
completed with expected statuses and no KASAN report, Oops, or panic.

The reproducer and complete guest configuration are available privately
to maintainers on request.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ceph: fail readdir when the MDS reply carries no dirfrag

A ceph mount oopses in ceph_readdir() when the MDS answers a READDIR
request with a reply whose extra blob is empty.  parse_reply_info()
skips reply blobs whose length is zero, so parse_reply_info_readdir()
never runs, r_reply_info.dir_dir stays NULL, and the reply still
parses as successful.  ceph_mdsc_do_request() returns 0 and
ceph_readdir() then reads rinfo->dir_dir->frag with no NULL check:

	/* extra */
	ceph_decode_32_safe(&p, end, len, bad);
	if (len > 0) {
		...
		err = parse_reply_info_extra(&p, p + len, req, features, s);
		...
	}

The oops on v7.3.0-rc4-00537-ga3ff15db6820, one getdents64(2) on the
mount root after an ms_mode=legacy mount, trimmed:

BUG: KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000000-0x0000000000000007]
Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xdffffc0000000000: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN NOPTI
CPU: 1 UID: 0 PID: 266 Comm: ls Tainted: G                 N  7.3.0-rc4-00537-ga3ff15db6820 #1 PREEMPT(lazy)
RIP: 0010:ceph_readdir+0xbff/0x3ea0
Call Trace:
 <TASK>
 ? __pfx_ceph_readdir+0x10/0x10
 wrap_directory_iterator+0xa2/0xe0
 iterate_dir+0x1da/0x5d0
 __x64_sys_getdents64+0x13b/0x2a0
 do_syscall_64+0xdd/0x4a0

The unconditional frag read came in with 81c6aea5275ea ("ceph: handle
frag mismatch between readdir request and reply"), so the bug is old.

Treat a reply with no dirfrag as a protocol violation: warn once,
drop the request and return -EIO, the same way ceph_readdir() already
handles the two malformed-reply cases later in the function.

Tested on v7.3.0-rc4-00537-ga3ff15db6820 (KASAN).  Unpatched, the
getdents64(2) above takes the machine down (oops=panic) on the first
READDIR reply.  With the patch it warns once and getdents64(2)
returns -EIO, no oops, no hang.  A conformant reply for an empty
directory — dirfrag present, zero entries, FRAG_END|FRAG_COMPLETE —
still lists "." and ".." and returns EOF on both kernels, so normal
readdir behavior is unchanged.  The oops is still present in
v7.3-rc5 (72d3fcf802c45).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

blk-crypto: fix NULL deref and UAF in __blk_crypto_evict_key()

Sashiko reported a possible NULL pointer dereference, triggered by the
following flow:

  dm-inlinecrypt ctor            # first use of the fallback
   ├─ blk_crypto_init_key()      # succeeds, ctx->key.size != 0
   ├─ blk_crypto_start_using_key()
   │   ├─ hw-wrapped key: -EOPNOTSUPP
   │   │    # profile never allocated (NULL)
   │   └─ raw key: fallback_start_using_mode()
   │      └─ blk_crypto_fallback_init() fails
   │         └─ kfree(profile)   # not NULLed
   ├─ goto bad
   └─ inlinecrypt_dtr()          # evicts whenever key.size is set
      └─ blk_crypto_evict_key()
         └─ blk_crypto_config_supported_natively() = false
            └─ blk_crypto_fallback_evict_key()
               └─ __blk_crypto_evict_key(blk_crypto_fallback_profile)
                  └─ profile->num_slots # BOOM!!!

This issue can be reproduced using the following commands:

  dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/backing bs=1M count=64
  LOOP=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/backing)
  SZ=$(blockdev --getsz $LOOP)
  KEY=$(head -c 64 /dev/urandom | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')
  dmsetup create ic --table "0 $SZ inlinecrypt aes-xts-plain64 \
    $KEY 0 $LOOP 0 1 keytype:hw-wrapped"

And the following oops is triggered:

  ==================================================================
  blk-crypto: loop0: no support for wrapped keys
  Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address
        0xdffffc000000000b: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI
  KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000058-0x000000000000005f]
  CPU: 5 UID: 0 PID: 901 Comm: dmsetup 7.3.0-rc3 #1 PREEMPT(lazy)
  RIP: 0010:__blk_crypto_evict_key+0x2e/0x3b0
  Call Trace:
   blk_crypto_evict_key+0x24c/0x320
   inlinecrypt_dtr+0xf6/0x160
   inlinecrypt_ctr+0x2d3/0xbd0
   dm_table_add_target+0x661/0xf40
   table_load+0x1c4/0x490
   ctl_ioctl+0x32f/0x5f0
   dm_ctl_ioctl+0xe/0x20
  ==================================================================

dm-inlinecrypt is the only caller that can evict a key that was never
started, as fscrypt frees such a key without evicting it.

Fix this by returning early from blk_crypto_fallback_evict_key() when
tfms_inited[] is not set for the key's mode.  tfms_inited[] is only set
after blk_crypto_fallback_init() has successfully initialized the
profile, so the crash above is no longer reachable.

The bug has been latent since commit c984ff1423ae ("blk-crypto:
dynamically allocate fallback profile") was merged in v6.5, and only
became actually triggerable when commit e7f57d2c47e2 ("dm-inlinecrypt:
add target for inline block device encryption") was merged in v7.2.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ARM: 9524/1: mm: align hugetlb mappings to the huge page size

mmap(MAP_HUGETLB) on 32-bit Arm can return an address which is not
aligned to the huge page size. In a QEMU virt guest, unmapping the VMA
then hits the alignment check in __unmap_hugepage_range():

  kernel BUG at mm/hugetlb.c:5213!
  Internal error: Oops - BUG: 0 [#1] SMP ARM
  PC is at __unmap_hugepage_range+0x540/0x584
  LR is at __zap_vma_range+0x13a0/0x1410

Commit 7bd3f1e1a9ae ("mm: make hugetlb mappings go through
mm_get_unmapped_area_vmflags") made hugetlb mappings use the
architecture's arch_get_unmapped_area(). The generic implementations
handle hugetlb alignment, but the Arm implementations only account for
the optional SHMLBA cache-colouring constraint. A 4 KiB-page kernel can
therefore align the mapping to 4 KiB or 16 KiB instead of the required
2 MiB.

Set the alignment mask from the file's hstate for hugetlb mappings in
both Arm implementations. Huge-page alignment also satisfies the
SHMLBA constraint.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: mt76: mt7925: fix reset panic caused by the WM2 rx irq mask

mt7925_irq_map sets wm2_complete_mask, but mt7925_dma_layout has no
tx done ring, so the MT_RXQ_MCU_WA queue and its NAPI are never set up.
On a chip reset, mt7925e_mac_reset() calls napi_disable() on that NAPI
and crashes:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000a40
  Workqueue: mt76 mt7925_mac_reset_work [mt7925_common]
  RIP: 0010:mutex_lock+0x1c/0x50
  Call Trace:
   napi_disable+0x1d/0x50
   mt7925e_mac_reset+0x327/0x420 [mt7925e]
   mt7925_mac_reset_work+0x9a/0x1a0 [mt7925_common]

Remove the WM2 mask from mt7925_irq_map and from
MT7925_INT_RX_DONE_ALL.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

fork: don't create io threads once PF_POSTCOREDUMP is set

zap_process() skips every thread that already has PF_POSTCOREDUMP set.
Such a thread is past synchronize_group_exit(), so a coredump can't
catch it anymore. It isn't counted in core_state->threads_remaining and
it isn't sent SIGKILL.

do_exit() sets PF_POSTCOREDUMP in synchronize_group_exit() and calls
io_uring_files_cancel() right after that. The cancellation runs task
work and a create_worker_cb() that io-wq queued before the exit creates
a new io-wq worker from there. If another thread started a coredump in
the meantime that worker joins a thread-group which is already being
dumped. zap_process() never saw it so it was never counted. But when it
exits it sees signal->core_state in synchronize_group_exit() and
decrements threads_remaining like any other thread.

So the count reaches zero one thread early and the dumper leaves
coredump_wait_inactive() while a thread it counted is still running.

The task has no fatal signal pending because zap_process() deliberately
didn't send it one, and it never went through get_signal() so it doesn't
have PF_SIGNALED either.

Refuse to create an io thread when the creator has PF_POSTCOREDUMP.
That costs nothing. io_uring_files_cancel() raises IO_WQ_BIT_EXIT
before it runs any task work, so a worker created from there only ever
gets to exit again, and io_should_retry_thread() doesn't retry -EINTR.

Clearing PF_POSTCOREDUMP for the new thread in copy_process() was the
other option. It makes the worker a thread like any other, but it only
helps while the dump hasn't started. A worker born after zap_process()
has run is invisible to it whatever its flags say and still decrements
threads_remaining on the way out. Refusing to create it covers both, and
then no task is ever born with the flag, so there is nothing to clear.

Moving io_uring_files_cancel() ahead of synchronize_group_exit() closes
the same window. It runs the cancellation, and whatever that can block
on, before the thread announces itself to the dumper. A thread that
blocks there never reaches coredump_task_exit() at all, so the dumper
ends up waiting for a thread that never parks. Refusing the creation
leaves the cancellation where it is. But it's very ugly to run io_uring
work even before we did all the generic exit work.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: reject FSCTL_SET_ZERO_DATA on a directory handle

An authenticated client with a writable tree connection can open a
directory with FILE_WRITE_DATA and send FSCTL_SET_ZERO_DATA on that
handle. The handler only checks fp->daccess & FILE_WRITE_DATA_LE, but on
a directory FILE_WRITE_DATA is the legitimate add-file right, so the
check passes. ksmbd_vfs_zero_data() then calls kernel_write() on the
directory file, which has no FMODE_WRITE, and __kernel_write_iter()
hits WARN_ON_ONCE(!(file->f_mode & FMODE_WRITE)), panicking a
panic_on_warn kernel.

Before commit 25e414db7033 ("ksmbd: report holes in allocated range
queries") the dense-file path used vfs_fallocate(), which rejects
directories with -EISDIR. The kernel_write() loop that replaced it has
no such check. Reject a directory handle in ksmbd_vfs_zero_data() before
writing, as ksmbd_vfs_write() already does for SMB2_WRITE.

  WARNING: fs/read_write.c:608 at __kernel_write_iter+0x74b/0x8c0
  Workqueue: ksmbd-io handle_ksmbd_work
  Call Trace:
   kernel_write+0x1ef/0x4d0
   ksmbd_vfs_zero_data+0x413/0x590
   smb2_ioctl+0x21fa/0x66a0
   handle_ksmbd_work+0x61b/0x1ff0

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: release failed pending sockets of a listener

A child of a listener only left the listen.pending or listen.ready
list via smbdirect_socket_accept() or when the listener was
destroyed. So every connection that failed before it was accepted
(negotiate timeout, peer disconnect, invalid negotiate request, ...)
stayed on the list and counted against the backlog until the listener
was destroyed. After about backlog (10 for ksmbd) such connections
smbdirect_listen_connect_request() rejected every new connection with
-EBUSY, so an unauthenticated peer was able to permanently stop
ksmbd from accepting SMB-Direct connections.

Now a failed child moves itself to a new listen.orphaned list at the
end of smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work(), after the disconnect was
started, and queues listen.purge_orphaned_work, which releases it
with smbdirect_socket_release(), without holding the listener's
rdma_lock_handler() lock, in the same way smbdirect_socket_destroy()
does for the remaining children. Orphaned sockets still count against
the backlog until they are released.

sc->accept.listener is now only changed under listener->listen.lock
and whoever clears it is responsible for releasing the socket:
smbdirect_socket_accept(), purge_orphaned_work or the destroy of the
listener.

In order to make that work:

- a struct smbdirect_socket that is a listener is now freed via
  kfree_rcu(), so that a child can dereference sc->accept.listener
  under rcu_read_lock(), even if the listener is released concurrently.

- smbdirect_listen_connect_request() adds nsc to the listen.pending
  list and sets nsc->accept.listener before it calls
  smbdirect_accept_connect_request(), and always returns 0 so the
  rdma_cm core keeps the connection id and nsc owns it. On a non-zero
  return it schedules nsc's teardown with
  smbdirect_socket_schedule_cleanup(), which orphans it off the
  listener so that purge_orphaned_work releases it; nsc destroys its
  own connection id with rdma_destroy_id() in that teardown. The
  teardown has to be deferred because the rdma_cm core holds nsc's
  id_priv->handler_mutex across the handler, so nsc->rdma.cm_id must
  not be destroyed synchronously from here. That same handler_mutex
  (and the listener's) also guarantees nsc can't go away under us,
  so setting the listener before the call is safe and lets a failure
  orphan nsc.

- smbdirect_accept_negotiate_recv_work() no longer moves a socket to
  the ready list if it already failed or no longer belongs to the
  listener. Every accepting socket has a listener, so if
  sc->accept.listener is already cleared, it no longer sends a
  negotiate response, as the socket is about to be released.

- smbdirect_socket_destroy() of the listener disables
  purge_orphaned_work and also releases the orphaned sockets.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: don't wait for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync()

smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync() waited for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED
after smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work() called rdma_disconnect(). That
can take very long, e.g. if the peer just disappeared, until the
rdma cm gives up, or forever if the event already happened, but the
status was overwritten afterwards.

This is not needed: smbdirect_socket_destroy() drains the qp under
rdma_lock_handler(), destroys it and calls rdma_destroy_id(), which
only waits for a currently running event handler and makes sure no
further events are delivered. The rest of the disconnect protocol
(DREQ/DREP and timewait for IB, abrupt close for iWarp) is handled
by the rdma core asynchronously. drivers/nvme/host/rdma.c also just
calls rdma_disconnect() and ib_drain_qp() before rdma_destroy_id().

So smbdirect_socket_destroy() now also accepts
SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTING and changes the status to
SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTED itself under rdma_lock_handler().

We could still get RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in the small
windows between rdma_unlock_handler() and rdma_destroy_id(),
but in that case smbdirect_connection_rdma_event_handler()
is basically a no-op.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: wait for negotiation before receiving another PDU

The receive thread queues a request and can read the next PDU before
the negotiation worker finishes. While need_neg is set, the next PDU
can cause ksmbd_init_smb_server() to replace conn->ops. A pipelined
SMB2 request can therefore make the worker handle an earlier, shorter
SMB1 request with SMB2 operations and read beyond its buffer.

An SMB1 multi-protocol negotiate may be followed by an SMB2 NEGOTIATE
that changes conn->ops again. Wait for work queued while the connection
is new or needs negotiation to complete before reading another PDU.
This keeps the operations stable for both stages of negotiation without
changing when need_neg is cleared.

littlefs 2.8.0 through 2.11.3 contains a divide-by-zero vulnerability in lfs_mount_() that allows attackers to crash processes mounting crafted filesystem images when block_count is 0. Attackers can supply an image lacking a superblock entry or recording block_count 0, causing lfs->seed % lfs->block_count to trigger SIGFPE and denial of service.

Improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic (Cypher injection) in the fulltext and vector index query generator of the sharded property database in Neo4j Enterprise Edition 2026.07.0 before 2026.10.0 allows an authenticated user holding ACCESS, CREATE INDEX and NAME MANAGEMENT privileges to inject Cypher that is accepted for execution on a property shard, in the session of any user who later queries the index, via a crafted index name containing a single quote. The impact is bounded by the privileges of the querying user.
Use of uninitialized memory when processing certain font files in X.Org libXfont before 2.0.10 could be used by authenticated attackers to crash the X server.

Mattermost Plugins versions <=12.-1 11.0.11 11.11.7 11.2.10.0 fail to check for a nil result after decoding the HTTP request body which allows an authenticated user to crash the Zoom plugin process, causing denial of service, via sending a JSON null body to the plugin's action endpoints. Mattermost Advisory ID: MMSA-2026-00722

Mattermost Plugins versions <=12.-1 11.0.11 11.11.7 11.2.10.0 fail to verify that the caller can post in a run's channel when executing a checklist slash command which allows an authenticated run participant to post arbitrary messages into a private channel they are not a member of via the checklist item run endpoint. Mattermost Advisory ID: MMSA-2026-00730

Mattermost Plugins versions <=12.-1 11.11.7 11.2.10 11.1.11.0 fail to enforce the GitLab project permission check for confidential issues when the project is publicly visible which allows an authenticated user with no GitLab membership in the project to obtain the contents of confidential issues, including title, description, author, and URL via subscribing a channel to the parent public GitLab group with the confidential_issues feature and waiting for a confidential issue webhook event. Mattermost Advisory ID: MMSA-2026-00738

United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP GetConfiguration Stack-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP messages. When parsing GetConfiguration requests, the process does not properly validate the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length stack-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-28968.

United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A Wi-Fi Configuration Server Missing Authentication Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to modify Wi-Fi configuration on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of Wi-Fi configuration requests. The issue results from the lack of authentication prior to allowing access to functionality. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-29068.

United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP Backend Configuration Authentication Bypass Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP backend configuration requests. The issue results from the lack of authentication prior to allowing access to functionality. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-29063.

United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A Download of Code Without Integrity Check Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP messages. The issue results from the lack of proper verification of firmware integrity prior to installation. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-28957.

United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP Backend Configuration Hard-Coded Credentials Authentication Bypass Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the configuration of the OCPP backend settings interface. The issue results from the use of hard-coded credentials. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-29056.

United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A FTP URL Path Parsing Stack-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of FTP URL paths during firmware updates. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length stack-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-28960.

United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP UpdateFirmware Out-Of-Bounds Write Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP UpdateFirmware requests. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in a write past the end of an allocated buffer. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-29487.
